retrieved_chunks_details.text: Database Management Systems: ACID Transactions and Concurrency Control A transaction in a database management system is a logical unit of database processing that includes one or more database access operations. Transactions must satisfy the ACID properties: 1. Atomicity: Either all operations of the transaction are executed and reflected in the database, or none are. Handled by the write-ahead logging (WAL) recovery manager. 2. Consistency: Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves database consistency invariants and integrity constraints. 3. Isolation: Even if multiple transactions execute concurrently, the system guarantees that for every pair of transactions T_i and T_j, it appears to T_i that either T_j finished execution before T_i started, or T_j started execution after T_i finished. 4. Durability: Once a transaction successfully commits, the updates made to the database persist even in the event of system crashes.

retrieved_chunks_details.text: Virtual Memory and Page Replacement Algorithms Virtual memory decouples the user's logical memory from physical memory, allowing execution of processes whose address spaces exceed available physical RAM. Memory is organized into fixed-size blocks called pages (in logical memory) and frames (in physical memory). When a process attempts to access a page not currently residing in physical RAM, the memory management unit (MMU) generates a page fault hardware interrupt. When a page fault occurs and all memory frames are occupied, a page replacement algorithm must select a victim frame to swap out: - FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Replaces the oldest page loaded in memory. Can suffer from Belady's Anomaly, where increasing the number of page frames results in an increased number of page faults. - Optimal (OPT / Belady's Min): Replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future. Provides the lowest page fault rate but is impossible to implement in practice because future references cannot be known. - Least Recently Used (LRU): Replaces the page that has not been used for the longest period in the past. Approximates the optimal algorithm by using past temporal locality.

retrieved_chunks_details.text: Computer Networks: Transport Layer Protocols and TCP 3-Way Handshake The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented, reliable, byte-stream transport layer protocol defined in RFC 793. Unlike UDP, which is connectionless and best-effort, TCP provides guaranteed in-order delivery, flow control, and congestion control. Before data transfer begins, TCP establishes a virtual connection between client and server using a Three-Way Handshake: 1. SYN: The active client generates a randomly chosen Initial Sequence Number (ISN_client = x) and sends a TCP segment with the SYN control flag set to 1. 2. SYN-ACK: The passive server receives the SYN segment, allocates connection buffers and state variables, generates its own Initial Sequence Number (ISN_server = y), and transmits a segment with SYN=1 and ACK=1, where the acknowledgment number is set to x + 1. 3. ACK: The client receives the SYN-ACK, transitions to the ESTABLISHED state, and transmits an ACK segment with ACK=1 and acknowledgment number set to y + 1. Data payloads can accompany this third packet.
